title: Splines for a yield curve
objectives: Fit a cubic spline through yields and read off rates between the quoted points.

screens.prose: Eight zero rates are quoted, continuously compounded, at 1 to 30 years. A client wants the 4-year and 15-year rates. The dashed curve joins the quotes with straight lines; the orange one is the degree-7 polynomial through them.
screens.question: Read the straight-line rates at 4 and 15 years.

hints.text: 4 years is halfway between the 3-year and 5-year quotes.
15 years is halfway between 10 years, 4.25%, and 20 years, 4.70%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the two quotes either side.

byKey.r0c1: Halfway between 3.90% at 3 years and 3.95% at 5 years.
byKey.r1c1: Halfway between 4.25% at 10 years and 4.70% at 20 years.

explain.text: Straight lines give 3.925% and 4.475%. The polynomial gives 3.9103% and 5.1921%, and $-2.58\%$ at 25 years: level 2's wiggles again. We want something smooth that stays near the quotes.

screens.prose: The blue curve is a **natural cubic spline**: a cubic on each interval. Value, slope and curvature match at every quote. Drag any quote up or down and watch the whole curve respond.
screens.question: Put the quotes back. What does the spline give at 15 years?

hints.text: Press Start over, then read the caption.
The caption shows the spline at 4 and 15 years.
At 15 years the spline gives 4.5297%.

feedback.correct: 4.5297%, between the straight line and the polynomial.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption with the quotes in place.

byKey.poly: That is the polynomial, which overshoots.

explain.text: The spline gives 3.9114% at 4 years and 4.5297% at 15. It bends smoothly through every quote without the polynomial's swings. Its curvature is zero at the two ends, which is what natural means.

screens.prose: Let $M_k$ be the spline's second derivative at knot $t_k$. Matching slopes at each inner knot gives $$h_{k-1}M_{k-1} + 2(h_{k-1} + h_k)M_k + h_kM_{k+1} = 6\left(\tfrac{y_{k+1} - y_k}{h_k} - \tfrac{y_k - y_{k-1}}{h_{k-1}}\right),$$ with interval lengths $h_k = t_{k+1} - t_k$ and $M_1 = M_8 = 0$.
screens.question: Find the right-hand side of the 5-year row, with rates in per cent.

hints.text: At 5 years, $h_{k-1} = 2$ (from 3) and $h_k = 2$ (to 7).

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the slope after 5 years minus the slope before, times 6.

byKey.sum: That is the 3-year row's value. Use the slopes either side of 5 years.

explain.text: Before 5 years the slope is 0.025 per year, after it 0.05, so the right side is $6 \times 0.025 = 0.15$. The diagonal entry is $2(2 + 2) = 8$. Six such rows make a tridiagonal system for $M_2$ to $M_7$, solved in $O(n)$ steps.

screens.prose: Solving the six rows gives the $M_k$, in per cent per year squared: $M_2 = 0.1372$, $M_3 = 0.0510$, $M_4 = 0.0033$, $M_5 = 0.0107$, $M_6 = -0.0047$, $M_7 = -0.0041$. `CubicSpline(t, z, bc_type="natural")` returns the same.
screens.question: Check the 2-year row: $4M_2 + M_3$ should equal its right-hand side. What is $4M_2 + M_3$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $M_2$ by 4 and add $M_3$.

byKey.noFour: You added $M_2$ and $M_3$ without the 4 on the diagonal.

explain.text: $4 \times 0.1372 + 0.0510 = 0.60$, the right side $6(-0.05 + 0.15)$. The big $M_2$ is the curve's dip at 3 years bending back up. Every row of the system checks the same way.

screens.prose: Swaps are priced off **forward rates**, $f(t) = z(t) + tz'(t)$. The spline's forwards are smooth: 4.0273% at 4 years, 5.2010% at 15. Straight-line zeros have a jump in slope at every knot.
screens.question: With straight-line zeros, what is the forward just above 5 years, in per cent?

hints.text: Above 5 years the line runs to 4.05% at 7, so $z' = 0.05$ per year.
$f = z + tz'$ with $z = 3.95$ and $t = 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the slope of the line from 5 to 7 years.

byKey.below: That uses the slope from 3 to 5 years, so it is the forward just below 5.
byKey.zero: That is the zero rate. The forward adds $t z'(t)$.

explain.text: Just below 5 years the forward is $3.95 + 5 \times 0.025 = 4.075\%$; just above, $3.95 + 5 \times 0.05 = 4.20\%$. A jump of 12.5 bp at a knot is a fake trade a swaps desk would see. The spline's forward has no jumps.

screens.prose: A colleague says moving one quote moves the curve only near that quote. Drag the 5-year quote up by 10 bp, from 3.95% to 4.05%, and read the caption.
screens.question: By how many basis points does the 15-year rate move?

hints.text: Drag the 5-year point to 4.05% and compare the 15-year reading with 4.5297%.
The caption moves from 4.5297% to about 4.5622%.

feedback.correct: About 3.25 bp, ten years away from the bump.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the 15-year rate before and after the drag.

byKey.local: You assumed the far curve stays put. A cubic spline is global: every $M_k$ changes.
byKey.full: The far curve moves, but by about a third of the bump.

explain.text: The 10 bp bump moves the spline 5.51 bp at 4 years and 6.42 bp at 6. It also moves it $-2.67$ bp at 8.5 years and $+3.25$ bp at 15. One changed $y$ changes every $M_k$.

screens.prose: A natural cubic spline solves one tridiagonal system for the $M_k$, then evaluates each piece $$s(x) = M_k\tfrac{(t_{k+1} - x)^3}{6h} + M_{k+1}\tfrac{(x - t_k)^3}{6h} + \left(\tfrac{y_k}{h} - \tfrac{M_kh}{6}\right)(t_{k+1} - x) + \left(\tfrac{y_{k+1}}{h} - \tfrac{M_{k+1}h}{6}\right)(x - t_k).$$
screens.question: All eight quotes lie on one straight line. What is the spline?

options.text: A curve that wiggles between the quotes
options.why: Every right-hand side is 0 when the slopes agree, so every $M_k$ is 0.

options.text: A single cubic through all eight
options.why: With all $M_k = 0$, each piece is linear, and they join into one line.
The natural ends already have $M_1 = M_8 = 0$; nothing bends.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the right-hand sides when all slopes are equal.

explain.text: Equal slopes make every right-hand side 0, so the system gives all $M_k = 0$. Each piece is then the straight segment, and the spline is the line. This is a good unit test for spline code.

screens.prose: Write the spline in NumPy, with rates as decimals. Build the tridiagonal system row by row, solve it, then evaluate the piece that holds $x$. The 4-year zero-coupon price is $100e^{-4z(4)}$.
screens.question: Complete `natural_spline_M`, `spline_eval` and `zero_price`.

hints.text: Row $k$ has $h_{k-1}$, $2(h_{k-1} + h_k)$ and $h_k$; skip the entries that fall outside the matrix.
Find the piece with `np.searchsorted(t, x) - 1`, clipped to 0 and `len(t) - 2`.
`zero_price` is `100 * np.exp(-T * spline_eval(t, y, natural_spline_M(t, y), T))`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test `natural_spline_M` on the three-point example first.

explain.text: The three-point case has one row, $4M_2 = 6(-1 - 1)$, so $M_2 = -3$. With the real quotes the 4-year price is £85.5169. Straight lines give £85.4704.

screens.prose: A rates desk builds its curve from quotes each morning and prices every swap off the forwards. A cubic spline gives smooth forwards, but one quote moves the whole curve.
screens.question: Why do many desks use a scheme such as monotone convex interpolation?

options.text: It keeps forwards smooth and positive while one quote moves the curve only nearby
It fits the quotes more exactly than a spline
options.why: A spline already passes through every quote exactly.
Speed is not the issue: a spline is a tridiagonal solve.

options.text: It is a single smooth polynomial
options.why: A single polynomial would bring back Runge's swings.

hints.text: Compare the two columns for each scheme.
A hedger wants a 5-year bump to move only nearby rates.
Monotone convex trades a little smoothness for local response and sensible forwards.

feedback.correct: Smooth enough forwards with local response.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the spline lacks.

explain.text: A 10 bp bump at 5 years moved the 15-year rate 3.25 bp, spreading hedges across the book. Monotone convex interpolation keeps forwards positive and continuous, and a bump stays near its quote. Curve schemes are chosen for the forwards they produce.

ideas: A natural cubic spline is a cubic on each interval, matching value, slope and curvature at each knot, flat-ended.
Its second derivatives solve one tridiagonal system, so it costs $O(n)$ and never shows Runge's swings.
A spline is global: a 10 bp bump at 5 years moved the 15-year rate by 3.25 bp.
summary.trap: One quote does not move the spline only nearby. Every $M_k$ depends on every quote.

quiz.prose: A cubic spline joins cubic pieces at the knots.
quiz.question: What must match where two pieces meet?

options.why: That is a piecewise cubic with kinks. A spline also matches slope and curvature.
Matching the third derivative too would make it one cubic.
That is a Hermite cubic. A spline also matches the second derivative.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A spline is smooth to the second derivative.

explain.text: Matching value, slope and second derivative leaves two free conditions, fixed by the natural ends $M_1 = M_n = 0$. Matching the third derivative too would leave no freedom at all.

quiz.prose: The 4-year zero rate is 3.925% by straight lines, continuously compounded.
quiz.question: What is the 4-year zero-coupon price per £100?

byKey.annual: You compounded annually. These rates are continuously compounded.

explain.text: $100e^{-0.157} = £85.4704$. The spline's 3.9114% gives £85.5169, a difference of 4.65p per £100. On a large book that is real money from the interpolation choice alone.

quiz.prose: A spline through $n$ knots has $n - 2$ inner-knot equations for $n$ unknowns $M_k$.
quiz.question: What do the two natural end conditions say?

options.text: $M_1 = M_n = 0$: no curvature at the ends

options.why: That is the clamped spline with zero slope, a different choice.
The end values are the quotes themselves.

options.text: The third derivative is 0 at the ends
options.why: That is the not-a-knot idea, not the natural one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Natural means the ends do not bend.

explain.text: Natural end conditions set $M_1 = M_n = 0$, so the curve runs straight off each end. That closes the system to $n - 2$ equations in $n - 2$ unknowns.
